https://www.politico.eu/article/serbia-l.text: Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has dissolved his country’s parliament and announced snap elections for the end of October as he seeks to assert control over the febrile political situation in the country. “I am convinced that the citizens of Serbia will choose the right path into the future,” Vučić said Wednesday, adding that “preserving our democratic system” and avoiding divisions were his priorities. The snap elections will take place on Oct. 25, according to reports in Serbian media . Vučić acknowledged “turbulence” in Serbian society but blamed “significant interference by foreign powers” for inspiring student-led anti-corruption protests that have fueled the country’s political turmoil over the past two years. Advertisement Advertisement Demonstrations erupted after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024 , killing 16 people. Protestors have demanded accountability over the disaster and called for early parliamentary elections. On Monday, Prime Minister Đuro Macut asked Vučić to dissolve parliament and call fresh elections. “If we want to mitigate tensions in society there is no better way than to ask people,” Macut said . Vučić, who has been in power as ‌president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced calls to step down since the 2023 parliamentary elections, amid allegations of electoral fraud. His second and final term as president is set to end in 2027 and his powers will not expire with the dissolution of parliament. In June, Vučić said he would resign as president “within weeks,” but his ambitions to remain in power continue. His Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) has nominated him for prime minister if the party secures a majority in the upcoming snap election. Serbia has been a candidate for EU membership since 2012, but its bid has stalled over concerns about democratic backsliding in Belgrade and its refusal to sanction Russia for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

http://www.australiannews.net/news/27934.text: Home Asia Pacific News International News Business News Search News Network As Russia Tests Western Alliance, US Lawmakers Push NATO Shield Bill RFE 03 Oct 2026, 04:43 GMT+ WASHINGTON -- As tensions between NATO and Russia intensify amid growing fears of confrontation, US lawmakers are raising questions over the relationship between the United States and the military alliance. That is the issue at the center of a new bipartisanbillled by Democratic lawmaker Jimmy Panetta and his Republican counterpart Joe Wilson. TheNATO Shield Actwould require congressional approval before a president could initiate a US withdrawal from NATO. SEE ALSO: Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans Panetta, in an interview with RFE/RL on October 1, argued that the measure is particularly important at a moment when Russia is testing the alliance and uncertainty surrounds Washington's future force posture in Europe. The legislation, introduced September 24, would require the president to consult Congress within 72 hours of considering a withdrawal from the military alliance and submit a report explaining the legal basis, strategic rationale, and expected consequences. Any withdrawal action would end after 30 days unless Congress approved it. Panetta said NATO is one of the most consequential and successful security alliances in the history of the world and argued that any fundamental change in US national security policy should not be left to the president to decide. But his argument goes beyond the possibility of a formal US withdrawal. Panetta said Russian President Vladimir Putin is already testing NATO through pressure, probing, and poking at the alliance before any potential move toward direct confrontation. He pointed to Russia's activities around the Baltic region, Poland, and other NATO border states as examples of what he described as gray-zone warfare. For Panetta, the danger lies partly in actions that remain below the threshold of open war. We cannot let gray-zone warfare go unnoticed and unresponded to, he said, warning that Russia could gradually pressure NATO members in much the same way China has applied pressure around Taiwan. An attack on one of us will be an attack on all, Panetta said, invoking the alliance's collective-defense principle laid out in Article 5 in NATO's founding treaty.
